note:
The preface moves quickly through the necessary background (time, place, and source of conflict), setting the stage for the scenes that follow.

**1:1 In the days when the judges ruled.** The period of the judges in Israel was infamous as a time of instability and apostasy. The final verse of the book of Judges summarizes the moral quality of the time: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judg. 21:25).

**a famine.** Famine in ancient Israel was a common calamity: Abraham fled to Egypt due to a famine (Gen. 12:10); Jacob led the Hebrews to Egypt because of a severe famine (Genesis 42–45). Famines were often understood as a sign of God’s displeasure (Lev. 26:18–20; 1 Kin. 17:1). The occurrence of a famine at this time reflects Israel’s overall disobedience and unfaithfulness during the period of the judges.

**Bethlehem in Judah.** This city lies in the tribal region of Judah. This distinctive name first occurs in the final chapters of Judges (17:7–9; 19:1, 2, 18) and in the opening verses of Ruth (vv. 1, 2). Bethlehem means “house of food,” but at this point the house of food is empty.

**to sojourn.** A technical term in antiquity for someone living as an alien in a foreign land. It describes the social standing of one who works in a foreign country but has few of the rights and privileges of a native citizen.

**country of Moab.** Lit. “fields of Moab.” Moabites, who were related to Israel through Lot (Gen. 19:37), occupied parts of central Transjordan at various times. Although God protected them at first from the Israelite invaders (Deut. 2:9), the Moabites were subjugated by Saul (1 Sam. 14:47) and then by David (2 Sam. 8:2). See also Deut. 23:3. There were some periods of friendly relations, with considerable cultural and economic interchange, as shown by David’s placement of his parents with the king of Moab while he was a fugitive (1 Sam. 22:3). During the period of the judges, in which the book of Ruth takes place, there were times of hostility between Israel and Moab (see Judg. 3:12–30).

Lit. “my God is king.” There is irony in the fact that Elimelech’s actions belie his name: he does not trust God, his king, to provide for him in the Promised Land, and so he moves to a pagan land where he dies. The ensuing drama emphasizes the role of the women in the family as they demonstrate the trust in the Lord that Elimelech lacked (4:14, 16).

**Naomi.** Lit. “pleasant/sweet” (vv. 20, 21). Naomi’s story is told first.

**Mahlon and Chilion** . Like their father, Mahlon (lit. “illness”) and Chilion (lit. “destruction”) die outside the Promised Land.

These marriages are ill-advised. Biblical law demands that the Israelites not intermarry with pagan peoples (e.g., Deut. 7:1–4). The irony is that an heir, and an ancestor of the great king David, will come through one of these foreigners. God will take these questionable marriages and redeem them for His own glory and purposes.

**Orpah.** The meaning of this name is not certain, but it may be related to “stubborn,” which is consistent with Orpah’s decision to stay in Moab.

**Ruth.** This name sounds like the Hebrew word for “friend,” and Ruth’s actions epitomize covenant friendship.

Naomi is an elderly widow, a sojourner in a foreign land, with two Moabite daughters-in-law who are also widows and childless. She is completely empty at this point and seems an unlikely prospect for any role in the Lord’s covenantal history of redemption.

These verses set the stage for vv. 8–18. The women must decide what factors will determine their paths: finding a husband and having children, living in one’s own country, being close to one’s family, or (finally, for Ruth) trusting in the sovereign Lord of Israel and the only true God. Naomi’s love for her daughters-in-law and her reaction to bitter experiences at God’s hand dominate this scene. Ruth’s decision and her irrevocable vow of fidelity to Naomi’s people and her God say much about the impact of Naomi’s character and faith on her daughter-in-law.

**1:6 the Lord** **had visited his people.** A note of hope is sounded. Ruth’s story never loses sight of God, whose faithful love determines history.

**1:7 to return.** The verb “to return” occurs twelve times in Ruth 1:6–22. While it is commonly used in Hebrew of a person changing a course of action and physically returning to a place, it can also describe a spiritual renewal. It is used in the OT for a person who repents and turns back to God (e.g., Hos. 3:5; 6:1; 7:10). Its repetition in the text of Ruth likely indicates that the characters are not merely returning to the Land of Promise but also turning to Yahweh.
This initial declaration of both daughters heightens the dramatic tension., 10

Naomi’s talk of raising up sons to replace the missing husbands only exaggerates her loss. The idea itself may refer to the law of levirate marriage. According to this law, if a man dies leaving a widow, his brother is obligated to marry the widow, taking his place and preserving the family line (Deut. 25:5, 6). The term “levirate” derives from the Latin _levir_, which means “husband’s brother.” There is also a custom that when someone dies, a close relative (or redeemer) is supposed to buy (or redeem) the deceased’s estate (2:20 note).
LORD **has gone out against me.** Naomi understands that no matter what happens to her, good or ill, her circumstances are playing out according to the providence of God.

A new element is introduced. It becomes clear that the choice of homeland is a choice for or against the true God. Against the background of Orpah’s choice, the courage and beauty of Ruth’s declaration (vv. 16, 17) are all the more obvious.

verse_quote: where you go I will go.
note: This verse includes four constructions known as _idem per idem_, a literary device in which the same verb or noun is used of one person’s actions and then of another person’s actions. It is used to underscore the intensity of the action as well as the totality of commitment.

As noted in 1:2, Naomi’s name means “sweet.” She does not want to be called this anymore because this name does not reflect her current life situation. She now wants to be called “Mara,” a Hebrew word meaning “bitter” (cf. 1:13).

She is not just any Ruth. For the story it is crucial that she be remembered as a foreigner (1:4; 2:2, 6, 21; 4:5, 10; esp. 2:10). Also, the reader is prompted to think of Ruth’s ancestor, Lot’s daughter, and the incestuous beginnings of the Moabite nation (Gen. 19:30–38). In both cases, the problem is childlessness or lack of a male heir.

**barley harvest.** Early calendars, like the Gezer calendar from the tenth century B.C.., associated months with the agricultural cycle. Barley was the first of the cereals to be harvested, in April; wheat was the last. In later tradition the barley and wheat harvests came to be identified with the festivals of Passover and Pentecost. The season of harvest was a time of celebration, rejoicing together before God, and remembering the poor. The narrative development is tied to this scheme. The women return home at the barley harvest, a time of God’s favor and the beginning of fruitful restoration for Naomi.

Ch. 2 introduces the last main character, Boaz, and the major theme, that of the close relative, or redeemer, who has certain responsibilities for the family and property of a relative who dies (2:20 note). The narrator, who already knows what is ahead, gives only a hint with the description of Boaz as “a relative” in v. 1. Only after the natural kindness of Boaz and the natural winsomeness of Ruth have taken their course does Naomi reveal the key to the entire story: Boaz is “a close relative” (2:20). Even then, no claims are made; there is no appeal to custom. Events must wait their time; while Naomi plans, Ruth serves quietly, and Boaz finishes the harvest. However, God had already provided an answer through the law (Leviticus 25).

**2:1 relative.** Or “acquaintance.” The Hebrew text leaves the technical status of Boaz unclear, but the story unfolds as if he is the one described in Lev. 25:25 as the “nearest redeemer,” whose responsibility relates primarily but not exclusively to the property of an impoverished relative (1:11; 2:20 and notes). Later (2:20; 3:9), Boaz will be identified as a “close relative,” but at this point he is introduced to prepare the reader for the events that place Ruth in his field.

**worthy.** This Hebrew word describes someone powerful and important in society.

**Boaz.** Lit. “in him is strength,” and Boaz shows himself to be a man of strong covenant character.

verse_quote: Let me go to the field.
note: Ruth’s initiative, on the surface, is simply to keep herself and Naomi alive, according to a custom codified in Leviticus (19:9, 10; 23:22) and Deuteronomy (24:19). As poor people, Ruth and Naomi will receive some help, but much more is about to come their way. A hint of this provision is given in Ruth’s plaintive request that she might glean “after him in whose sight I shall find favor.”
From Ruth’s perspective, where she ends up working is mere happenstance. However, in reality, all is unfolding according to the mysterious providence of God.
Boaz’s arrival satisfies the expectations raised in vv. 1–3.

The servant’s answer establishes Ruth’s character. She is faithful, having come while still in her youth to a foreign country for the sake of her mother-in-law. She is hardworking, having been busy since morning.

**2:7 among the sheaves.** Ruth’s request is within the bounds of her right as a widow (Deut. 24:19–21). But Boaz’s response will go far beyond the legal requirement (v. 15), thereby demonstrating his generosity.

**except for a short rest.** Lit. “This is her dwelling; the house is little.” “This” refers to the field, and it has been her residence all day long. The “house” in town has meant “little” to her. Ruth is diligent and industrious, spending so much time at work in the field that it has become her “home.”

Events unfold quickly as Boaz accedes to the request and offers his protection and provision (vv. 8, 9). Ruth acknowledges his favor to her, an undeserving “foreigner” (v. 10). Only then does the narrative give some inkling of God’s providential working (vv. 11, 12). Boaz already knows that Ruth is no ordinary foreigner. She has taken “refuge” under the “wings” of the Lord, and she will receive “a full reward” from Him (v. 12). Though a foreigner, Ruth’s loyalty to God is a key element in God’s great plan of redemption. The plan will be worked out through two of Ruth’s descendants: David, the covenant king, and Christ, David’s greatest son. The reward of Ruth’s faith far transcends local time and circumstances.
There is a wordplay here, as the term “foreigner” is related to the verb “to take notice of.”
A frequent image of safety and protection in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 61:4; 63:7; 91:4).

Boaz’s permission is clearly extraordinary.

**2:14 wine.** A sour but refreshing drink or dip (cf. Num. 6:3).

Beating out the grain, or threshing it, separates the kernels from the husks, chaff, and stalks. An ephah is a measure of dry capacity equal to three-fifths of a bushel, or about thirty pounds (13 kg) of barley.

verse_quote: what food she had left over.
note: What she set aside from her noon meal (v. 14).

God is faithful, and He will not forget the ones He loves. The blessings He promises will pass from Boaz to Ruth to Naomi, and eventually to all the elect.

**close relative of ours.** The law of redemption now comes into view. According to this law, the nearest male blood relative has the duty of preserving the family name and property. This duty might entail avenging the death of a family member (Num. 35:19–21); buying back family property that was sold to pay debts (Lev. 25:25); buying back a relative who sold himself into slavery to pay debts (Lev. 25:47–49); and levirate marriage, marrying the widow of a deceased relative (Deut. 25:5–10). Apparently, these duties can be renounced or declined under certain circumstances (cf. Ruth 3:12; 4:1–8). Boaz is such a “close relative” (or “redeemer”) to Ruth, and this fact now determines the course of action (1:11; 2:1 and notes). Ruth’s destiny will proceed according to the law, unlike that of her ancestor, Lot’s daughter, who committed incest (Gen. 19:30–38).

verse_quote: until the end of the barley and wheat harvests.
note: The time of Ruth’s labor amounts to approximately three months in the fields.

Now the narrative moves toward resolution. In a late-night visit, Ruth carries out and expands Naomi’s plan, putting her own reputation and all her expectations at risk. She claims the protection of Boaz as a “redeemer” (v. 9). Her trust in his character is vindicated, and she is unharmed. God’s activity behind the scenes continues without a break. But even at this moment, the engagement must be delayed; there is a closer relative (3:12), and Boaz, a man of outstanding honor, will not rest until this obstacle is removed.

**3:1 rest for you.** This means that Ruth should be married, a need that Naomi has taken to heart (1:9).

A cleared area where grain is crushed or torn to separate the chaff, straw, and grains. The harvest is then winnowed, or thrown into the air for the wind to blow away the chaff as the grains fall directly to the ground. All this takes place in the spring at the time of the harvest festivals.

A highly symbolic act. By coming to the threshing floor and lying at Boaz’s feet, Ruth is asking Boaz to marry her. She is, in effect, saying she wants to be redeemed, and she awaits Boaz’s judgment in the matter.

**lie down.** Ruth lies patiently at Boaz’s feet until he awakens (vv. 8, 9); nothing unseemly happens between them during the night (v. 11).

Boaz has been drinking but is hardly drunk. He is content and fulfilled with his day’s labor and his evening meal. After all the work of the day, Boaz goes to “the end of the heap of grain,” a place where Ruth is able to meet him privately. God’s providence is clearing a path for her.

verse_quote: Spread your wings over your servant.
note:
Boaz has wished for protection for Ruth under God’s wings (2:12); Ruth now gives Boaz the opportunity to be the answer to his own prayer. See text note. Ezek. 16:8 explains the idiom. Ruth asks directly for the favor of marriage, although Naomi’s instructions were not quite so bold (v. 4).

**redeemer.** The law does not specify marriage as the responsibility of such a person, though an extension of Leviticus 25 can readily be envisioned. Mahlon’s name and property will be preserved (4:10), suggesting the levirate marriage, but it is difficult to see how Deut. 25:5, 6 can be strictly applied.

Lit. “covenant love.” Throughout the book, God’s own covenant love (1:8; 2:20) is mirrored by that of Ruth (1:8, 16, 17). Now her faithfulness is proved as she invokes the duties of a close relative and declines to follow any of the young men. The “kindness” Boaz refers to is evidently Ruth’s proposal to follow the custom that will provide an heir for Naomi.

**the first.** When she chose to accompany Naomi.

The feminine equivalent of the Hebrew phrase in 2:1. Ruth has risen from being a Moabite and servant to becoming attractive to Boaz as a possible marriage partner. In the Hebrew canon, the book of Ruth follows the book of Proverbs. In the last section of Proverbs, the author asks, “A worthy woman who can find?” one whose “works praise her in the gates?” (Prov. 31:30, 31). The answer is immediate in the Hebrew canon: Boaz has found a “worthy woman” who is praised in the gates, one who is known for her selflessness and her covenant love for Naomi (2:8–13).

Boaz suddenly mentions a complicating factor. Hebrew law appears to mandate an order of rank of kinsman-redeemers (Lev. 25:47–49), and there is a closer kinsman than Boaz who has the first right of acceptance or refusal. The custom of redemption seems to be leading to a solution, but now it creates a problem along the way. The engagement must be postponed.

This gift of barley shows Boaz’s magnanimity toward Ruth (v. 17) and is a symbol of Naomi’s changed estate (1:21). Ruth receives grain from Boaz as an emblem of her future fruitfulness.

**Then she went into the city.** Lit. “Then he went into the city.” The latter makes perfectly good sense: as soon as Boaz gives his word to Ruth, he goes directly into Bethlehem to fulfill his oath.
The same Hebrew words are translated “Who are you?” in v. 9.
The grain serves as a token and pledge not only to Ruth but also to Naomi. It is a visible sign of a promise.
This is an ironic touch, for the time to wait will be very short. Naomi does not expect a conclusion to be long in coming.

Ch. 4 brings out the divine purpose behind Ruth’s original decision to follow Naomi and Naomi’s God. The necessary arrangements seem to turn on a combination of levirate marriage regulations (Deut. 25:5–10) and the laws for a redeeming relative (Lev. 25). Ruth is taken as a wife, and ancient blessings for fruitfulness are invoked. Naomi’s bitterness turns to joy, and her grandson is shown to be the grandfather of King David. In these events the Lord’s hidden providence is revealed.

**4:1 the gate.** Excavations at Iron Age Israelite sites have revealed a number of gateways with built-in benches where the elders sat in judgment (e.g., Megiddo and Gezer). The city gates were an area of economic activity.

**friend.** Boaz must know the man’s name, but the narrator quotes Boaz as referring to the man with an indefinite phrase, something like the English expression “Mr. So-and-So.” Because the other names in the book are related to one’s character, it is likely that this man has no name because he has no character. For the purposes of the story, he is “Mr. No Name.”

There is no recorded legal requirement for a particular number of men. The later Jewish tradition by which ten men make up a quorum for worship may derive from this incident. In a rural culture, where the use of writing was limited, it was important for a contract to be made with a number of official witnesses.

This sale is a surprising new element, no hint of which has been given up to now. Details about the sale are not necessary for the story and are omitted. A parallel example can be seen in Jer. 32:6–15.
Little is known about the symbolism of this custom. Its point clearly is to confirm the transaction legally. See Deut. 25:9, 10 (a different setting) and Amos 8:6.

verse_quote: to perpetuate the name of the dead.
note: The OT considers the disappearance of one’s name an extreme misfortune (1 Sam. 24:21; 2 Sam. 14:7).

These are the two wives of Jacob (Israel), the mothers, either naturally or through their maids Zilpah and Bilhah, of all the sons of Israel, the heads of the twelve tribes.

**Ephrathah ... Bethlehem.** As in 1:1, 2, these place names, associated with David, are given special prominence.

In a much earlier time, Judah became the father of Perez because Onan refused to carry out his obligation as a close relative (Gen. 38:29). Perez is a symbol of the fruitful offspring. In the same way, Boaz becomes the father of Obed (v. 21) because another person has refused to carry out the levirate obligation. Despite human failures, the messianic line is preserved (Matt. 1:3, 5, 16). Interestingly, strong parallels exist between Tamar and Ruth, both of whom are women and foreigners who play key roles in continuing the messianic line.
LORD **gave her conception.** This statement underscores the providence of God in the story.

The women’s praises celebrate the fulfillment of God’s covenant love to Naomi. Her daughter-in-law Ruth is more to her than seven sons would be (v. 15). Moreover, Naomi in effect has a son in her grandson Obed (v. 17). He will become the grandfather of David. Remarkably, the infant Obed is described by the women of Bethlehem as a redeemer. This implies that the line of Boaz is associated with the concept of redemption. Ultimately, Jesus Christ is the Redeemer of the world.

This is probably not a formal rite of adoption. Rather, it is a symbol that Naomi views the child as her own in a manner of speaking. He is the heir of Elimelech’s estate and the continuation of her husband’s lineage.
Lit. “servant,” because he will serve Naomi in her old age.

The closing genealogy is almost exactly what is recorded in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt. 1:3–6. The book of Ruth finds its climax in the coming of the Messiah, Jesus Christ. The main characters, Boaz and Ruth, have faded from the story. The emphasis is now on the lineage that points to Christ. The coming of the Messiah is the end-all of the book of Ruth.

Here and in v. 17, the author mentions ancient Israel’s greatest king explicitly. We are not to view the book of Ruth as merely a story of honorable people in a dishonorable era, but as the account of God’s providence and grace in providing a king who gives rest to His people Israel (2 Sam. 7:1–17). Of course, David fails to give Israel permanent rest, but in providing a son for Naomi, the Lord also preserves a lineage that births David’s greatest son, Jesus Christ, who gives rest to all who trust in Him (Matt. 11:28–30).
